does: Cooks a flat piece of food in a thin layer of hot fat, turning it once.

intro.what: Pan-frying cooks a flat piece in a thin layer of hot fat.
intro.why: It teaches you to leave the surface in contact with the pan long enough to develop colour before turning.

how: Heat a film of fat in the pan over medium heat.
Lay the food in, away from you, and leave it alone.
Turn it once, when the underside is golden and it lifts without sticking.
For an egg, keep the heat gentle and spoon hot fat over the white until it is set.

cues.text: A steady, gentle sizzle. Spitting means the heat is too high or the food is wet.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the food again and again, so that it never browns.
mistakes.fix: Turn it once. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.

quiz.question: Why leave a flat piece undisturbed at first when pan-frying?
choices: To give the underside time to brown.
To let the underside absorb as much fat as possible.
quiz.because: Steady pan contact lets the underside develop colour before it is turned.

quiz.question: How is the pan prepared for this method?
choices: Fill it deeply enough to submerge the food.
Heat a thin film of fat over medium heat.
Start with a dry cold pan and no fat.
quiz.because: A film of hot fat supports shallow surface cooking rather than deep-frying.

quiz.question: Which sound suits gentle pan-frying?
quiz.because: A gentle sizzle fits the intended moderate heat; spitting can point to excess heat or surface water.

quiz.question: Repeated turning is interrupting browning. What should change?
choices: Let the underside colour before turning.
Keep lifting and pressing the piece.
quiz.because: Giving the surface uninterrupted pan contact allows colour to develop instead of repeatedly disturbing it.

variant_of.differs: Larger, flat pieces that lie still and are turned once, over gentler heat.
